title: Strategy I: Setting Course (External Analysis)
sources: M03 Handout Lecture Slides BA-A (30 p.)

bigPicture: Average profitability differs strongly **between industries** (median operating margins FY2021–2025). Why?

**Strategy** serves to gain and maintain a **competitive advantage**: unique positioning, choices about what not to do, differentiation, sustainable value capture, long-term commitments. **Operational effectiveness is not a strategy** (Porter); a good strategy has a **kernel**: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action (Rumelt).

**Porter's Five Forces** (industrial organization economics) explain why some industries are more profitable: threat of new entry, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitution, industry rivalry. ASML illustrates a very strong position.
The wider **PESTEL** environment and **M&A** (e.g. Bayer–Monsanto) can put competitive advantage under pressure.
Firms try to **tame competition** (build an **economic moat**); regulators try to **increase competition**: their goals are **polar opposites**.

concepts.name: Recap of Lecture 2 and motivation
concepts.simple: Last time: firms cooperate to create value. Now: why are some industries (like tech) much more profitable than others (like energy)?
concepts.exam: Recap: companies collaborate to create value (Williamson's graph); cooperation requires governance mechanisms (Grünenthal termination right); platforms help govern large-scale collaboration. Motivation: **median operating margins by sector (FY2021–2025)** differ widely (energy, utilities, materials, industrials, communication services, consumer staples, consumer discretionary, health care, information technology). The question: **why do industries differ in average profitability?** → external analysis.
concepts.example: Strategy is about **capturing** value (course map: organizing = why firms exist; strategy = capture value).

concepts.name: What strategy is (and is not)
concepts.simple: Strategy means choosing a special place in the market and deciding what you will NOT do, so customers come to you and not to others. Just doing the same things a bit faster is not a strategy.
exam: Strategy serves to **gain and maintain a competitive advantage**:
- **Activities designed to achieve unique market positioning**;
- **Decisions about what to do and what not to do**;
- **Differentiation** from competitors;
- **Capturing value in a sustainable way**;
- **Long-term commitments** that are often **irreversible**.
**Operational effectiveness is not a strategy!** Slide 6: Porter identifies **three major mistakes** in defining strategy (video).
concepts.example: Cutting costs 5 % like every rival = operational effectiveness; deciding to serve only premium customers and drop the rest = strategy.

concepts.name: A good strategy: Rumelt's kernel
concepts.simple: A good strategy first says what the real problem is, then picks a general approach, then lists actions that fit together.
concepts.exam: A good strategy **identifies the key challenge that needs to be overcome**. The **core (‘kernel’) of strategy** (Rumelt): **(1) rich diagnosis** (what is going on, what is the key challenge?), **(2) guiding policy** (the overall approach to deal with it), **(3) coherent action** (coordinated steps that implement the policy).
concepts.example: Mock exam B1: name and explain the three kernel elements (3 points).

concepts.name: Example: ASML
concepts.simple: ASML, a Dutch company, is the only firm in the world that builds the super-complex machines needed to print the tiniest computer chips.
concepts.exam: ASML (Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography): founded **1984**; semiconductor industry; customers are **chip manufacturers**; one **EUV lithography machine costs ≈ USD 300–400 m**. **Extreme ultraviolet (EUV)** light can carve very small structures; it **cannot be focused like lasers**, **exists only in a vacuum**, and requires **mirrors so smooth that deviations are on the order of individual atoms**. Question: how did it become Europe's most valuable technology company?
concepts.example: Mock exam case: Canon and Nikon also make lithography machines, but not EUV; ASML's optics come from a close partnership with Zeiss.

concepts.name: Porter's Five Forces (industrial organization economics)
concepts.simple: Five pressures decide how much money an industry lets firms keep: new competitors coming in, powerful suppliers, powerful customers, other products doing the same job, and fighting among existing rivals. The weaker the pressures, the more profit.
concepts.exam: Porter's model explains **why some industries are more profitable than others**: **threat of new entry** (emergence of new rivals), **supplier power** (bargaining power of critical suppliers), **buyer power** (bargaining power of key customers), **threat of substitution** (alternative products), with **industry rivalry** (competitive intensity) in the centre. Average industry profitability tends to be **highest when the five forces are weak**.
concepts.example: Mock exam A1: profitability is highest when the forces are **weak** (not strong).

concepts.name: Threat of new entry
concepts.simple: If it's cheap and easy to start a rival business (an app instead of a fleet of cars), new competitors will rush in.
concepts.exam: The threat of new entrants is **high** when: **switching costs for customers are low**; **capital requirements are low**; **retaliatory measures are unlikely**; established companies do **not** have **proprietary technology**, **established brands**, **exclusive distribution channels**. Example **Uber vs. taxis**: low capital requirements (an app instead of a company-owned fleet), low switching costs for passengers, virtually no proprietary technology (MyTaxi rebrands as ‘Free Now’).
concepts.example: Mock exam A2: low customer switching costs **increase** the threat of entry; proprietary technology, high capital needs and likely retaliation lower it.

concepts.name: Supplier power
concepts.simple: If only a few suppliers have what you absolutely need and you can't switch, they can charge you a lot.
concepts.exam: Suppliers have strong bargaining power when: **forward integration** poses a credible threat; there are **no substitutes** for the supplier's products; the products are **differentiated**; established firms face **high switching costs**; the product is an **important input** for the buyer. High: **rare earths** (concentrated reserves, China leading). Low: farmers selling to the **few major food retail chains** (Feuerborn: “only four major food retail chains… if, as a farmer, I don't agree to the price terms, I won't be able to sell my produce”).
concepts.example: Mock exam A3: from the retail chains' perspective, the farmers' complaint illustrates **high buyer power** (the chains are the buyers).

concepts.name: Buyer power
concepts.simple: Customers are powerful if there are few big ones, if the product is the same everywhere, if switching is free and if they know all the prices.
concepts.exam: Buyers have strong bargaining power when: there are **few, large buyers**; buyers purchase **large quantities** relative to a seller's size; products are **standardized**; buyers face **little or no switching costs**; **backward integration** is credible; the buyer has **complete information**. Example **electricity via Verivox/Check24**: many small private households (normally a sign of low buyer power), **but** a **standardized product**, **comprehensive information** through comparison websites (platforms) and **virtually no switching costs** (automated switching, sign-up bonuses) → **high** buyer power.
concepts.example: Mock exam C2 asks exactly this argument (3 points).

concepts.name: Threat of substitution
concepts.simple: A substitute is a different product that does the same job: car-sharing instead of owning a car.
concepts.exam: Substitutes **meet the same customer need in a different way**. The threat is high when: the substitute offers **good value for money**; **switching costs** to the substitute are **low**. Example: **buying a car in a big city**: high purchase and maintenance costs vs. mobility benefits; **car-sharing** is generally well developed in major cities with **low switching costs** (just app registration).
concepts.example: Mock exam A4: for car manufacturers, car-sharing is a **threat of substitution**.

concepts.name: Industry rivalry
concepts.simple: When many similar firms fight in a market that isn't growing and can't easily leave, they cut prices and spend heavily: everyone earns less.
concepts.exam: Rivalry = competition for **market share and industry profits**. High when: **many competitors**; companies **similar in size**; **slow industry growth or shrinking** industry; **high exit barriers**; **contractual obligations** exist; **geographic or historical ties** exist; products and services are **direct substitutes**. Example: the **“streaming wars”** (Netflix, Prime, Disney+, Paramount+, Apple TV, HBO Max, RTL+).
concepts.example: Mock exam B2: rivalry = same product, existing competitors; substitution = different product, same need.

concepts.name: Application: ASML's Five Forces
concepts.simple: ASML is hard to copy and has no substitute, so it's very strong, even though its few big customers and key suppliers are powerful too.
exam: | Force | Slide facts | Assessment |
| Threat of new entry | technological complexity, patent protection, high capital requirements, established customer relationships | **low** |
| Supplier power | specialized components, few key suppliers, high switching costs, long-term relationships | **high** |
| Buyer power | concentrated, large customers with significant bargaining power, **but** ASML's technology is central to their production | **mixed / high but limited** |
| Threat of substitution | no comparable technology, industry standards built around ASML, patent protection | **low** |
| Industry rivalry | few, but a strong incentive for those involved; rapid technological change | **low (few rivals in EUV)** |
Headline: **ASML is in a strong position due to the high barriers to entry.**
concepts.example: Mock exam C1 (8 points): assess four forces for ASML with case facts.

concepts.name: PESTEL: the sociopolitical environment
concepts.simple: Around the industry there's a bigger world: politics, the economy, society, technology, nature and laws, all of which can help or hurt a firm.
exam: Layers: **firm → strategic group → industry → PESTEL environment**.
| Dimension | Examples on the slide |
| **Political** | government policy, political stability, fiscal policy |
| **Economic** | economic growth, exchange rates, interest rates |
| **Social** | population, demographics, lifestyle |
| **Technological** | technology development, automation, R&D activities |
| **Environmental** | weather, climate, environmental policy |
| **Legal** | labour law, consumer protection, occupational safety and health law |
concepts.example: Mock exam A5: labour law and consumer protection = **Legal**.

concepts.name: M&A as market consolidation; Bayer–Monsanto
concepts.simple: Buying a competitor removes a rival, so the industry becomes less competitive. But it can go badly wrong, as Bayer found after buying Monsanto.
concepts.exam: According to Porter's model, **M&As reduce competition and concentrate market power** (e.g. top-10 agrochemical firms, 2015). **Failed M&A:** Bayer bought **Monsanto**; Bayer's share price plummeted and a **wave of lawsuits** (Roundup) hit the company. CEO Bill Anderson: “We are slowly reaching a point where the litigation industry could force us to stop marketing this system-critical product.” Lessons: **competitive advantages are repeatedly called into question**; **even though market competition decreased, the hoped-for increase in profitability did not materialize**.
concepts.example: Less rivalry on paper ≠ higher profits in practice.

concepts.name: Taming competition: the economic moat
concepts.simple: A moat is the water around a castle that keeps attackers out. A firm's ‘moat’ is whatever keeps competitors from stealing its profits.
concepts.exam: Companies have an interest in **taming competition** to generate higher profits → **sustainable competitive advantage** = an **economic moat**. Five sources: **intangible assets**, **cost advantage**, **switching costs**, **network effects**, **efficient scale**. Reference: Peter Thiel, “**Competition is for losers**” (*Zero to One*).
concepts.example: Mock exam A6: ‘high industry growth’ is NOT a moat source.

concepts.name: Politics and strategy: regulation vs. corporate strategy
concepts.simple: Firms want less competition (higher prices); regulators want more competition (lower prices). Their goals pull in opposite directions.
concepts.exam: **Regulatory bodies are interested in increasing competition to lower prices.** Examples: EU fines **Apple and Meta ≈ €700 m**; **New York City's crackdown on Airbnb**; the European Commission **prohibits HeidelbergCement and Schwenk's takeover of Cemex Croatia**. **Punchline:** (1) strategy aims to create and maintain a competitive advantage; (2) the five forces shape it; (3) **the goals of corporate strategy and regulation are polar opposites**.
concepts.example: In Porter's logic firms want weak forces (moats, consolidation), regulators want strong forces (entry, rivalry) → opposite goals.

connections: **Microeconomics 2.1 ↔ BA 3:** the market-structure taxonomy (monopoly, oligopoly, polypoly) and the buyer/seller perspective (monopsony) underlie the Five Forces; the welfare loss of market power explains why regulators fight it.
**Lecture 2 → 3:** network effects and winner-takes-all reappear as a **moat** source; platforms (Verivox, Check24) raise buyer power.
**Lecture 1 → 3:** switching costs and hold-up ↔ supplier power and buyer power.
**Lecture 3 → 4:** Five Forces = external, market-based view; Lecture 4 adds the internal, resource-based view; **non-substitutability** (VRIN) ↔ threat of substitution.

questions: What strategy is and is not (Porter); Rumelt's kernel.
Name the five forces and the determinants of each; classify statements (e.g. low switching costs → higher threat of entry).
Apply the Five Forces to a case (ASML-style), with facts for each force.
Explain why buyer power can be high with many small buyers (electricity comparison platforms).
Economic moat and its five sources; why strategy and regulation are polar opposites.
traps: Profitability is highest when the forces are **weak**.
Low switching costs **raise** the threat of entry and of substitution, and raise buyer power.
The farmers–retailers quote: from the **retailers'** viewpoint = **high buyer power**.
Car-sharing for car manufacturers = **substitution**, not rivalry.
Many small buyers usually mean **low** buyer power, unless standardized products, full information and zero switching costs.
M&A reduces rivalry but doesn't guarantee higher profits (Bayer).
mistakes: Listing forces without case facts (mock exams demand justification).
Mixing up supplier power and buyer power perspectives.
Naming ‘high industry growth’ as a moat source.

memorize: **Strategy:** unique positioning; what to do and not do; differentiation; sustainable value capture; long-term, often irreversible commitments. Operational effectiveness ≠ strategy.
**Rumelt's kernel:** diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action.
**Five forces:** threat of new entry, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitution, industry rivalry.
**New entry high:** low switching costs, low capital requirements, unlikely retaliation, incumbents lack proprietary technology/brands/exclusive channels.
**Supplier power high:** credible forward integration, no substitutes, differentiated products, high switching costs, important input.
**Buyer power high:** few large buyers, large volumes, standardized products, low switching costs, credible backward integration, complete information.
**Substitution high:** good value for money, low switching costs.
**Rivalry high:** many and similar-sized competitors, slow growth, high exit barriers, contractual obligations, geographic/historical ties, direct substitutes.
**PESTEL:** political, economic, social, technological, environmental, legal.
**Economic moat sources:** intangible assets, cost advantage, switching costs, network effects, efficient scale.
gaps: Slide 6 (Porter's **three major mistakes** in defining strategy) and slide 7 (Rumelt) rely on **videos**; the PDF doesn't list the three mistakes.
The slides don't explain the five moat sources one by one (only the labels).

The ASML slide lists facts per force without explicitly saying ‘high’ or ‘low’; the assessments in the table above are derived from the headline (‘strong position due to high barriers to entry’) and the facts.
Slide 29 is missing from the handout numbering.

questions.question: According to Richard Rumelt, a good strategy has a ‘kernel’ of three elements. Name them and briefly explain each.
questions.model: (1) Diagnosis: identifies and explains the key challenge the firm must overcome (what is going on?). (2) Guiding policy: the overall approach chosen to deal with that challenge. (3) Coherent action: coordinated, mutually consistent steps that put the guiding policy into practice.

keyPoints.text: Guiding policy named and explained (overall approach)
Coherent action named and explained (coordinated steps)

questions.question: Explain what an economic moat is and how it relates to sustainable competitive advantage. Name three of its sources and briefly describe one of them.
questions.model: An economic moat is a firm's protection against competitors, like a moat around a castle: it lets the firm ‘tame competition’ and keep earning high profits over time. A moat is therefore the basis of a sustainable competitive advantage. Sources (lecture): intangible assets, cost advantage, switching costs, network effects, efficient scale. E.g. network effects: the product becomes more valuable as more people use it, so new rivals struggle to attract users (winner-takes-all).

keyPoints.text: Moat defined (protection against competitors / taming competition)

questions.question: ASML is the only company producing EUV lithography machines (≈ USD 300–400 m each, a few dozen per year). EUV light exists only in a vacuum and requires mirrors with atomic-scale precision. Canon and Nikon make lithography machines, but not EUV. ASML's optics come from a close partnership with Zeiss. Assess (high/low, with case facts) for ASML: (a) threat of new entry, (b) supplier power, (c) buyer power, (d) industry rivalry.
questions.model: (a) Low: extreme technological complexity (vacuum, atomic-precision mirrors), patents, very high capital requirements, established customer relationships. (b) High: specialized components and few key suppliers (e.g. Zeiss optics), high switching costs and long-term relationships. (c) Mixed/high but limited: customers are few, large, concentrated chip manufacturers with significant bargaining power, but ASML's EUV technology is central to their production and has no alternative, which limits their power. (d) Low: in EUV there is no direct rival (Canon/Nikon only non-EUV); few players, though rapid technological change keeps a strong incentive to compete.

keyPoints.text: (a) Low, with at least two case facts
(b) High, with justification (few key suppliers, Zeiss, switching costs)
(c) Concentrated powerful buyers BUT dependence on ASML → limited
(d) Low (no EUV rival; Canon/Nikon not EUV), with justification

questions.question: Explain the statement ‘the goals of corporate strategy and regulation are polar opposites’ using Porter's logic, with one example from the lecture.
questions.model: Porter: industry profitability is high when the five forces are weak. Firms therefore try to tame competition, e.g. through moats or consolidation via M&A, to capture higher profits. Regulators aim to increase competition to lower prices for consumers, e.g. by blocking mergers or fining dominant firms. Example: the European Commission prohibited HeidelbergCement and Schwenk's takeover of Cemex Croatia (or EU fines on Apple and Meta, NYC's crackdown on Airbnb).

keyPoints.text: Firms want weak forces / tamed competition → higher profits
Regulators want more competition → lower prices
